mcqs.question: Two unrelated processes, started independently with no common parent, need to communicate using a pipe-like mechanism. Which should they use?
options: An anonymous pipe, since any process can open one by PID
A named pipe (FIFO), since it exists as a filesystem path any process can open without a shared ancestor
Neither — pipes always require a parent-child relationship
An anonymous pipe, but only if both processes were started by the same shell
mcqs.explanation: Anonymous pipes rely on inherited file descriptors from a common ancestor (typically via fork), so unrelated processes can't use one directly. A named pipe (FIFO) is created as a filesystem entry that any process with path access can open, sidestepping that requirement entirely.

mcqs.question: After forking to set up a pipe, a child process reads from the pipe expecting end-of-stream once the parent finishes writing, but the read() call never returns even after the parent's write completes and the parent closes its write end. What's the likely bug?
options: The pipe buffer is too small to ever signal end-of-stream
read() on a pipe never returns 0, so this behavior is expected regardless
The child itself failed to close its own inherited copy of the write end, so the kernel still sees an open writer and won't signal end-of-stream
fork() does not actually duplicate pipe file descriptors into the child
mcqs.explanation: Both processes inherit both ends of the pipe from fork(); if the child doesn't close the write end it doesn't use, the kernel still considers a writer open (the child's own copy) even after the parent closes its copy, so read() blocks waiting for a write or EOF that never comes. fork() does duplicate the descriptors, and buffer size isn't the issue here.

mcqs.question: Why is shared memory the fastest IPC mechanism, and what does that speed cost you?
options: It's fastest because the OS batches and compresses messages automatically; the cost is higher CPU usage for compression
It's fastest because access after setup requires no kernel involvement or copying, like ordinary memory access; the cost is that the OS provides no automatic synchronization, so you must add your own
It's fastest because it always runs on a dedicated CPU core; the cost is that only two processes can ever use it at once
It's fastest because it skips virtual memory translation entirely; the cost is it can only be used between a parent and its direct children
mcqs.explanation: Once mapped, shared memory access is just ordinary memory access — no kernel call, no copying — which is why it's the fastest option. The cost is that the OS provides zero built-in coordination, unlike a pipe or queue's implicit blocking behavior, so concurrent access needs its own synchronization. No compression, dedicated-core, or parent-child requirement is involved.

mcqs.question: You need to send a 10KB JSON payload from one process to another. Should you use a signal to do it?
options: Yes, signals are the fastest way to send any amount of data
No — signals carry essentially no payload and are meant for notifying that an event occurred, not for transferring application data; use a pipe, socket, or shared memory instead
Yes, as long as you split the JSON into multiple signals
No — signals can only be sent to child processes, never to unrelated processes
mcqs.explanation: Signals are event notifications identified by a small integer, carrying essentially no payload — they're the wrong tool for transferring real data of any size. Signals can be sent to any process you have permission to signal, not just children; the issue is payload capacity and purpose, not addressing.

mcqs.question: You need two unrelated processes on the same machine to exchange a continuous, very high-throughput stream of large binary buffers, and you're prepared to handle synchronization yourself for maximum speed. Which IPC mechanism fits best?
options: A message queue, for its built-in message boundaries
Signals, for their minimal overhead
Shared memory, since it avoids the kernel-copy overhead that pipes, queues, and sockets all pay
A TCP socket, since it works across machines too
mcqs.explanation: Shared memory is the only option with zero per-transfer kernel copies, making it the right fit for maximum throughput when you're willing to add your own synchronization. The other options all pay real per-transfer costs (copies, per-message overhead, or network-stack overhead) that shared memory avoids.

mcqs.question: Two processes share a memory region: one writes a struct's three fields one at a time, and the other reads all three fields whenever it wants, with no synchronization in place. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing — shared memory writes are always atomic across all fields at once
The reader can observe a torn/partially-updated struct, reading some new field values and some stale ones, exactly like an unsynchronized race between threads
The OS will automatically block the reader until the writer finishes all three fields
This is only a risk if the two processes are on different machines
mcqs.explanation: The OS provides no coordination for shared memory access — it's exactly as unsafe as unsynchronized shared memory access between threads. A reader can see an inconsistent mix of old and new field values if it reads mid-write. There's no automatic blocking, and this has nothing to do with being on different machines (shared memory is same-machine only anyway).
